actions.justification: Mandatory first-line assessment for any pediatric patient. The Pediatric Assessment Triangle evaluates appearance, work of breathing, and circulation to skin to rapidly identify life-threatening conditions.
Mandatory assessment to interpret vitals using age-appropriate normal ranges for pediatric patients. Adult norms do not apply to children.
Mandatory for all pediatric patients. Weight in kg is required to calculate weight-based medication dosing and fluid volumes accurately.
MANDATORY action - establishing IV or IO access is critical for medication administration and fluid resuscitation. Must be completed within 60-minute deadline.
Assessing mental status is essential in pediatric patients to evaluate neurological function and guide further management.
Hypoglycemia is common in pediatric emergencies and can present with various symptoms; point-of-care glucose check is rapid and essential to rule out hypoglycemia as a contributing factor.
Mandatory fluid resuscitation with normal saline at 20ml/kg per pediatric shock/resuscitation guidelines. Must be completed within 60-minute deadline — 30 minutes remain.
Mandatory monitoring of urine output to assess end-organ perfusion and fluid resuscitation adequacy. Target urine output in pediatric patients is 1 ml/kg/hr.
Mandatory reassessment after fluid bolus administration to evaluate clinical response, guide further fluid management, and detect complications such as fluid overload.
Broselow weight estimation is essential for accurate weight-based dosing of all medications in this pediatric patient, including epinephrine, antihistamines, and corticosteroids.

Epinephrine IM is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis in pediatric patients. Given the available action set suggesting an allergic/anaphylaxis scenario, epinephrine should be administered promptly even with currently stable vitals to prevent deterioration.
H1 antihistamines (e.g., diphenhydramine) are adjunct therapy in anaphylaxis management after epinephrine, helping to reduce histamine-mediated symptoms.

Corticosteroids are recommended in anaphylaxis management to prevent biphasic anaphylactic reactions. Patient has been stabilized with epinephrine and fluids; corticosteroids are the next standard step.
Ensure reliable IV access is established for ongoing medication administration and fluid management, as prior access was IO/IV and a peripheral IV line should be confirmed.

Patient has received initial interventions (epinephrine, antihistamines, corticosteroids, NS bolus). With stable vitals (HR 80, BP 120/80, SpO2 98%), continuous close monitoring is essential to detect biphasic anaphylaxis reaction or clinical deterioration.

Second IV access provides additional vascular access for rapid medication or fluid administration if the patient deteriorates, particularly important in anaphylaxis management where repeated dosing may be needed.
Additional fluid support may be beneficial to maintain hemodynamic stability and ensure adequate perfusion, especially given prior anaphylactic reaction with potential vasodilation.
Continuous respiratory monitoring is essential post-anaphylaxis management to detect any late-phase bronchospasm or biphasic reaction. Patient has stable vitals but requires ongoing surveillance.
Basic metabolic panel to assess electrolytes, glucose, and renal function as part of ongoing workup and to guide further management in this post-anaphylaxis patient.
Blood gas analysis to assess oxygenation and ventilation status, ensuring no occult respiratory compromise in this anaphylaxis patient despite currently stable SpO2.

CBC is indicated to evaluate for infection, anemia, or other hematologic abnormalities that may be contributing to or complicating this patient's presentation. Labs are currently pending and additional diagnostic workup is appropriate.

Lactate level helps assess for tissue hypoperfusion or metabolic derangement, particularly relevant given prior fluid resuscitation and anaphylaxis management. Useful to confirm adequate perfusion despite currently stable vitals.
Supplemental oxygen is appropriate supportive care following anaphylaxis management to ensure adequate oxygenation, even with SpO2 of 98%, as a precautionary measure during monitoring phase.

Airway protection is a priority in any pediatric patient with anaphylaxis/acute allergic reaction who has received multiple interventions; ensures airway remains patent especially if angioedema or respiratory compromise develops.
